topics.title: Elevation of boiling point and depression of freezing point
topics.summary: Why a dissolved solute raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point, the molal constants, and how to get molar mass from each.

lessons.title: Elevation of boiling point
lessons.objective: Explain with a vapour-pressure graph why a solution boils at a higher temperature, use $\Delta T_b = K_bm$ to find a boiling point or a molar mass, and know when the equation is reliable.

blocks.text: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Water boils at 373.15 K because its vapour pressure there is 1.013 bar. A solution of a non-volatile solute has a **lower** vapour pressure at every temperature, so it must be heated **above** 373.15 K before its vapour pressure reaches 1.013 bar. Hence ==the boiling point of a solution is always higher than that of the pure solvent==. NCERT's example: 1 mol of sucrose in 1000 g of water boils at 373.52 K (see the note below on how this figure compares with $\Delta T_b = K_bm$).

blocks.caption: The solution's vapour-pressure curve lies below the solvent's, so it meets the 1.013 bar line at a higher temperature (after NCERT Fig. 1.7). The gap is exaggerated for clarity.
blocks.alt: Two vapour pressure curves against temperature with the boiling point elevation marked

blocks.label: Elevation of boiling point
blocks.where: $m$ = molality; $K_b$ = **boiling point elevation constant**, **molal elevation constant** or **ebullioscopic constant**, unit K kg mol$^{-1}$.
symbols: K (a change of 1 K = a change of 1 °C)
boiling points of solution and pure solvent
blocks.conditions: A dilute-solution relationship: the proportionality to molality holds well only when the solution is dilute (and ideal). For electrolytes multiply by $i$ (lesson 9.2).

blocks.label: Molality from masses, and molar mass
blocks.tex: m =  rac{w_2 	imes 1000}{M_2 	imes w_1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad M_2 =  rac{1000 	imes K_b 	imes w_2}{\Delta T_b 	imes w_1}
blocks.conditions: The 1000 converts the solvent's mass from grams to kilograms. The left equation is just the definition of molality; the right one inherits the dilute-solution condition from $\Delta T_b = K_bm$.

blocks.title: Boiling point of a glucose solution
blocks.problem: 18 g of glucose ($\ce{C6H12O6}$) is dissolved in 1 kg of water. At what temperature will it boil at 1.013 bar? $K_b$ = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$.
given: Glucose 18 g; molar mass 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180 g mol$^{-1}$
$K_b$ = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$; water boils at 373.15 K
blocks.why: The formula gives only the **rise**; the question asks for the actual boiling point.

convert.t: Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol; molality = 0.1 mol ÷ 1 kg = 0.1 mol kg$^{-1}$

calc.why: K kg mol$^{-1}$ × mol kg$^{-1}$ = K.
Add the rise to pure water's boiling point.

blocks.check: A dilute solution should boil only slightly above 373.15 K - it does.

blocks.title: Why does NCERT say 373.52 K for 1 mol of sucrose, when 0.52 K added to 373.15 K gives 373.67 K?

blocks.text: Using the chapter's equation for 1 mol of sucrose in 1 kg of water: $\Delta T_b = K_bm = 0.52 	imes 1 = 0.52$ K. Added to 373.15 K, that predicts **373.67 K**. NCERT's sentence says **373.52 K**, which is exactly 373 + 0.52 - so the sentence appears to add the 0.52 K rise to water's boiling point **rounded to 373 K**. NCERT does not say how the figure was obtained, so this is the most likely reading, not a confirmed one.

Two more cautions. First, 1 mol kg$^{-1}$ is not a very dilute solution, and $\Delta T_b = K_bm$ is a dilute-solution relationship, so neither 373.52 K nor 373.67 K should be read as a precise measured value. Second, the point of NCERT's sentence is qualitative: the solution boils **above** the solvent.

blocks.title: What to do in an exam
blocks.text: Use 373.15 K for water's boiling point, as NCERT Example 1.7 does, unless the question gives a different value - then use the question's value. If a question expects 373 K, the data will say so.

blocks.title: Molar mass from boiling point
blocks.problem: Benzene boils at 353.23 K. 1.80 g of a non-volatile solute in 90 g of benzene raises it to 354.11 K. $K_b$(benzene) = 2.53 K kg mol$^{-1}$. Find the molar mass.
blocks.relation: $M_2 = \dfrac{1000 	imes K_b 	imes w_2}{\Delta T_b 	imes w_1}$
blocks.why: The unknown is the molar mass, hidden inside the molality. This rearranged form puts it on its own.

calc.why: The 1000 turns 90 g of benzene into 0.090 kg inside the formula.

items: Lower vapour pressure → the solution must be hotter to reach 1.013 bar → higher boiling point.

lessons.title: Depression of freezing point
lessons.objective: Explain why a solution freezes at a lower temperature, use $\Delta T_f = K_fm$ to find a freezing point or molar mass, and report the answer as a temperature, not just a change.

blocks.text: The ==freezing point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of the substance in its liquid phase equals its vapour pressure in the solid phase==. A solution freezes when its vapour pressure equals that of the pure **solid solvent**. Because the solute lowers the liquid's vapour pressure, this equality is reached at a lower temperature: the freezing point falls.

blocks.caption: The solution's curve meets the frozen-solvent curve at a lower temperature than the pure liquid does (after NCERT Fig. 1.8). Not to scale.
blocks.alt: Vapour pressure curves of solid solvent, liquid solvent and solution with the freezing point depression marked

blocks.label: Depression of freezing point
blocks.tex: \Delta T_f = T_f^\circ - T_f = K_f\,m \quad\Rightarrow\quad M_2 =  rac{1000 	imes K_f 	imes w_2}{\Delta T_f 	imes w_1}
blocks.where: $K_f$ = **freezing point depression constant**, **molal depression constant** or **cryoscopic constant**, unit K kg mol$^{-1}$. The proportionality holds for dilute (ideal) solutions.
symbols: fall in freezing point (a positive number)
freezing points of pure solvent and solution
blocks.conditions: Dilute solutions; the solid that separates is pure solvent. For electrolytes multiply by $i$.

blocks.text: In calculations take the freezing point of water as **273.15 K** (NCERT's worked examples and the CBSE marking schemes do), even though Table 1.3 lists 273.0 K. A question giving '$K_b$ = 0.512' instead of 0.52 is fine - use the value given.

blocks.title: Antifreeze
blocks.problem: 45 g of ethylene glycol ($\ce{C2H6O2}$) is mixed with 600 g of water. Find (a) the freezing point depression and (b) the freezing point.
given: Ethylene glycol 45 g; molar mass 62 g mol$^{-1}$
$K_f$(water) = 1.86 K kg mol$^{-1}$; water freezes at 273.15 K
blocks.why: Freezing point **depression** means we subtract the change from the solvent's freezing point.

convert.why: Keep four figures here; rounding to 1.2 at this stage changes the final answer.

blocks.check: NCERT rounds the molality to 1.2 before multiplying and prints 2.2 K and 270.95 K. Keeping the extra digit gives 2.25 K and 270.90 K; both are accepted readings of the same calculation, and the difference shows why rounding should wait until the end.
blocks.answer: (a) 2.25 K  (b) 270.90 K (NCERT, rounding early: 2.2 K and 270.95 K)

blocks.title: Molar mass from freezing point
blocks.problem: 1.00 g of a non-electrolyte in 50 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 0.40 K. $K_f$(benzene) = 5.12 K kg mol$^{-1}$. Find the molar mass.
blocks.relation: $M_2 = \dfrac{1000 	imes K_f 	imes w_2}{\Delta T_f 	imes w_1}$
blocks.why: 'Non-electrolyte' tells us $i$ = 1: the particles are whole molecules.
blocks.check: A sensible molar mass for a molecular solid.

blocks.text: Salt sprinkled on snow-covered roads dissolves in the thin film of water and lowers its freezing point, so the ice melts at the road's temperature (asked in 2025 and 2026, 'name the colligative property': depression in freezing point). Ethylene glycol in car radiators works the same way.
$\Delta T_f$ is a *depression*. If $\Delta T_f$ = 1.55 K, the freezing point of the aqueous solution is 273.15 - 1.55 = 271.60 K (or -1.55 °C), not 1.55 °C.

items: The solution's lower vapour pressure meets the solid solvent's at a lower temperature.
Keep extra digits until the end; report a temperature with its unit.

lessons.title: The constants $K_b$ and $K_f$, and linking boiling and freezing data
lessons.objective: State what $K_b$ and $K_f$ depend on, read them from a table, and use one solution's molality to move between its boiling and freezing points.

blocks.label: Where $K_f$ and $K_b$ come from
blocks.tex: K_f =  rac{R 	imes M_1 	imes T_f^2}{1000 	imes \Delta_{fus}H}, \qquad K_b =  rac{R 	imes M_1 	imes T_b^2}{1000 	imes \Delta_{vap}H}
blocks.where: $M_1$ molar mass of solvent, $T_f$ / $T_b$ freezing / boiling point of the pure solvent in kelvin. So $K_f$ and $K_b$ depend only on the solvent.
symbols: enthalpies of fusion and vaporisation of the solvent
blocks.conditions: Derived for dilute solutions. Use $R$ in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ here because the enthalpies are in J mol$^{-1}$.

blocks.title: Why do the constants belong to the solvent?
blocks.text: Every quantity in these expressions describes the solvent: its molar mass, its melting or boiling point, its enthalpy change. The solute only supplies the molality. That is why doubling the molality doubles $\Delta T$ but leaves $K_b$ and $K_f$ unchanged.

blocks.title: From freezing point to boiling point
blocks.problem: An aqueous solution of a non-electrolyte freezes at −0.93 °C. At what temperature does it boil at 1.013 bar? ($K_f$ = 1.86, $K_b$ = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$)
given: $\Delta T_f$ = 0 − (−0.93) = 0.93 K (a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K)
blocks.find: Boiling point of the same solution.
blocks.relation: The molality is the same in both equations: $m = \Delta T_f/K_f$, then $\Delta T_b = K_bm$.
blocks.why: We are not told the solute, but we do not need it: molality links the two properties.
blocks.check: Shortcut: $\Delta T_b/\Delta T_f = K_b/K_f$, so $\Delta T_b = 0.93 	imes 0.52/1.86 = 0.26$ K.

items: $K_b$ and $K_f$ depend only on the solvent.
Unit of both: K kg mol$^{-1}$.
One solution, one molality: $\Delta T_b/\Delta T_f = K_b/K_f$.

questions.q: 9.0 g of glucose (180 g mol$^{-1}$) is dissolved in 250 g of water. Find the boiling point of the solution. ($K_b$ = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$; water boils at 373.15 K.)

mistakes.msg: You added the rise to 373 K. The question gives water's boiling point as 373.15 K.
You subtracted. A solute **raises** the boiling point: add $\Delta T_b$.

hints: You have the molality. Which equation gives the rise in boiling point?
$\Delta T_b = K_bm = 0.52 	imes 0.20$. Then add it to 373.15 K.

questions.q: 3.1 g of ethylene glycol (62 g mol$^{-1}$) is dissolved in 250 g of water. Find the freezing point of the solution. ($K_f$ = 1.86 K kg mol$^{-1}$; water freezes at 273.15 K.)

mistakes.msg: You added. A solute **lowers** the freezing point: subtract $\Delta T_f$ from 273.15 K.

hints: $\Delta T_f = 1.86 	imes 0.20 = 0.372$ K. Then subtract from 273.15 K.
